textbookText: Chapter 1 Physical Quantities Joseph Fourier (21 March 1768 – 30 May 1830) was a French mathematician and physicist. Fourier was born at Auxerre as a son of a tailor. He lost both his parents at the age of 9. He then went onto study at the Convent of St Mark. The concept of physical dimension, and of dimensional analysis was introduced by Joseph Fourier in 1822. The modern concept of dimension was introduced in 1863 by Clerk James Maxwell, who synthesized earlier formulations by Fourier.

Joseph Fourier (1768- 1830) 1.1 Introduction Think of different phenomena occurring in our nature: formation and disappearance of the clouds in the sky, appearance of a rainbow, rainfall, evaporation of pond water, strong wind or storm, cold dry winter, and hot summer. These are examples of physical or natural phenomena. A clear understanding of such phenomena requires some laws of physics, and these laws are expressed in terms of physical quantities. Length, time, mass, velocity, force, momentum, temperature, etc. are examples of physical quantities. The study of physics starts with the measurement of these diverse physical quantities. Hence, in this chapter, we focus on physical quantities and the need for their measurement.

Physics is the branch of science and is one of the most fundamental scientific disciplines. The main goal of physics is to understand how the universe functions. A scientist who specializes in the field of physics is called a physicist.
The word physics comes from the Latin word physica ('study of nature'), which itself is derived from the Greek term φύσις (phúsis ' meaning the origin, nature, property).
In Sanskrit, physics is called Bhautika, a physical world.

If a student looks around him/her, he/she finds desks, tables, benches, a board, a projector, a duster, and the school building. Beyond it, there are neighboring buildings, trees, vehicles on the road, and many more. All of these represent masses. If they are burnt, energy is released. The greater the mass, the more will be the energy liberated, and vice-versa. Apart from mass and energy, there is nothing around us. Hence, the entire universe is composed of only two things; mass and energy. Ultimately, the word ‘physics’ refers to the science of matter and energy and their interactions.

Physics is a quantitative science as it is based on the measurement that comes with numbers. Mathematics is used in physics to construct models aimed at predicting natural phenomena. Then these predictions are compared to the way the real world works. Physicists continuously strive to refine their models so that they can represent the world better. Physics studies very large things, as well as very small things. For instance, physicists cannot only study stars, planets, and galaxies but also small pieces of matter, such as atoms and electrons. They may also study about sound, light, heat, radioactivity, or even space and time. Physics not only helps people understand how objects move, but also how they change form, how they make sound, how hot or cold they will be, and what they are made of at the microscopic level. Physics is the branch of science that deals with the properties of matter and energy along with their interaction.
1.2 Physical Quantity A physical quantity is something that can be measured. For example, Mass = 87.5 kg, Length = 1.4 m, etc.
Physical quantities can be measured with instruments or can be derived.

Fig 1.2 Showing measurement of physical quantity All the measurable quantities from which the laws of physics are governed are the physical quantities. When we speak about something, say 2 hours journey, here '2 hours' refers to the physical quantity of time. Mass, length, time, temperature, velocity, acceleration, pressure, etc. are physical quantities. To understand them, one must measure and express them quantitatively in numerical values. This is done using units, which serve as standards of measurement. Physical quantities are expressed as multiples of these units. For example, the mass of a bag of apples is 5 kg, the distance is 200km, and the time is 2 hours. In all these, Physical Quantity = nu, where n is the numerical value of the physical quantity, and u is the unit of measurement. Physical quantities are of two types

1. Fundamental (or Basic) Quantities, 2. Derived Quantities Fundamental Quantities These are the physical quantities that are self-defined and independent of others. Examples are mass, length, time, temperature, illuminating power, electric current, and amount of a substance. Moreover, there are two sub-fundamental quantities; a plane angle and a solid angle.
